ghs.en: Taichi: "......"

rows.jp: そして今。
rows.en: And now.

ghs.en: And then, the present.
ghs.assessment: そして今 locates the narrative at 'and now.' Adding 'then' points to a different temporal relation.

rows.jp: 霧の言ったとおり、世界はあっさりとサッパリした。
rows.en: Just as Kiri had said, the world had been wiped clean without a fuss.

ghs.en: As Kiri had said, the world became clean and tidy so easily.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says the world was simply and thoroughly emptied or cleared out. 'Clean and tidy' domesticates this into neatness and misses the disappearance being described.

highlights.text: the world became clean and tidy

rows.jp: 人間なんて簡単に『なくなる』んだと、俺も思い知った。
rows.en: I too had learned how easily human beings could ‘disappear.’

ghs.en: And I realized as well that humans could just simply Pass Away.
ghs.assessment: The quoted なくなる means disappear or cease to exist. 'Pass away' narrows it to a euphemism for death and the arbitrary capitalization supplies emphasis not in the source.

rows.jp: アダムとイブとは言わないけど、せめてもう少し完璧な人間が生き残れば良かったのにな。
rows.en: I wasn’t asking for Adam and Eve, but it would have been nice if someone a little closer to perfect had survived.

ghs.en: I wouldn't say it should be like Adam and Eve, but it'd have been good if at least humans just a little bit more perfect had survived.
ghs.assessment: The English needs a quantified plural such as 'some humans' or a comparative noun phrase such as 'slightly more perfect people.'

highlights.text: at least humans just a little bit more perfect had survived

rows.jp: この二人は、もともと永遠に生きる完全性を備えていたが、善悪の知識の木から実を食べてしまったが故に罰せられ、不完全なものとされたんだ。
rows.en: Those two had once been perfect and could have lived forever. But they ate the fruit of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, and for that they were punished and made imperfect.

ghs.en: Those two, originally, had been provided with completeness, with the integrity to live eternally, but because they ate the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil and were therefore punished, they were made into something incomplete.

rows.jp: それでも千年生きたと記録されている。
rows.en: Even so, the record has them living a thousand years.

ghs.en: And yet, they are recorded to have lived a thousand years.

rows.jp: 聖書を追って読むと、子孫は世代を重ねるごとに寿命を縮めていったことがわかる。
rows.en: Read on, and their descendants' lifespans shrink with every generation.

ghs.en: If one continues with the reading of the Scriptures, it is possible to see how the lifespan of each successive generation decreases.

rows.jp: そして現代。
rows.en: And now, the modern age.

ghs.en: And then, this generation.
ghs.assessment: 現代 means the present day or modern era, not one biological generation.

rows.jp: 俺たちは、健全ささえ失いかけている。
rows.en: We are beginning to lose even our basic soundness.

ghs.en: We were losing even the soundness of mind.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese speaks about the narrator's current era and says 'we are even beginning to lose' soundness or health. The past progressive incorrectly places the condition in an earlier period.

rows.jp: こんな傷だらけの人間をとりわけて、神様はいったいどうする気なんだろう。
rows.en: What could God possibly mean to do with this particular collection of damaged human beings?

ghs.en: What could God possibly be thinking of doing by spreading around these humans so chock full of wounds?
ghs.assessment: とりわけて means singling out or selecting these wounded humans. The English instead says God distributes them spatially.

rows.jp: こんな……どす黒い感情を抱えた俺を。
rows.en: Me, nursing feelings this black.

ghs.en: Like me... so engorged in wicked feelings as I am.
ghs.assessment: A person can be engorged with something, not 'in' it, and the bodily image is not a natural rendering of harboring dark emotions.

rows.jp: どうせ世界は回っているのだと思った。
rows.en: I thought the world would keep turning no matter what.

ghs.en: I thought that the world was revolving anyhow,
ghs.assessment: The Japanese thought is that the world keeps turning no matter what. 'Was revolving anyhow' sounds like uncertain physical rotation and misses the concessive idiom.

rows.jp: 取り返しはきくのだと。
rows.en: That nothing was beyond repair.

ghs.en: and that it was possible to take back what was done.
ghs.assessment: 取り返しはきく means the damage can be undone or things can be set right. It does not mean retrieving an action already performed.

rows.jp: 極論①。
rows.en: Extreme Proposition No. 1.

ghs.en: Extreme argument #1.

rows.jp: 皆殺しにしても、全部リセット。
rows.en: Kill everyone, and it all resets.

ghs.en: All will be reset, even a massacre.

rows.jp: 記憶がなくなるオマケつき。
rows.en: Free memory wipe included.

ghs.en: With the disappearance of memories as lagniappe.

rows.jp: 発展性のない世界にあるのは、可能性という娯楽だけ。
rows.en: In a world with no future, possibility was the only entertainment left.

ghs.en:
A world in which advancement has no
consequence is a world that only has the
the amusement of the potential.
ghs.assessment: 発展性のない世界 is a world with no potential for development, in which possibility itself is the only amusement. The English instead says advancement has no consequence, duplicates 'the,' and preserves intrusive engine line breaks.

highlights.text:
A world in which advancement has no
consequence is a world that only has the
the amusement of the potential.

rows.jp: 俺はその悦楽を、思い描いてしまった。
rows.en: I found myself imagining the pleasure of it.

ghs.en: That was a pleasure I had well envisioned.
ghs.assessment: 思い描いてしまった says he ended up imagining that pleasure. 'Had well envisioned' introduces an unsupported past-perfect relation and uses 'well' as an unnatural aspect marker.

rows.jp: 鎌首をもたげる欲望。
rows.en: Desire reared its head.

ghs.en: Desire, like a snake, raises its head.

rows.jp: ゲームのはじまりを告げる。
rows.en: It marked the beginning of the game.

ghs.en: It proclaims the beginning of the game.

rows.jp: 「霧ちん、そこは新川豊が死んだ場所だよ」
rows.en: “Kiri-kins, this is where Yutaka Shinkawa died.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Kiri-chin, that's the spot where Shinkawa Yutaka died you know."
ghs.assessment: The diminutive Japanese address remains unexplained rather than being represented in English.

rows.jp: 霧は驚かなかった。
rows.en: Kiri did not look surprised.

ghs.en: Kiri was not surprised.

rows.jp: ゆるりと振り返る。
rows.en: She turned slowly.

ghs.en: She turns around, taking her time.
Taichi: "?"

rows.jp: 霧が驚かなかったことに、俺が少し驚く。
rows.en: Kiri's lack of surprise surprised me.

ghs.en: I was a little surprised at Kiri being unsurprised.

rows.jp: 「……世界がこんなことになって……人もいなくなって……」
rows.en: “...The world's come to this... Everyone is gone...”

ghs.en: Kiri: "...so the world came to be like this... where even people are gone..."

rows.jp: 「悪意はなくなったかわりに……密度もなくなって……」
rows.en: “The malice is gone... but so is the density...”

ghs.en: Kiri: "In exchange for malice being gone... its density is also gone..."
ghs.assessment: Kiri says that with malice gone, the density of the world or human existence has also vanished. The pronoun 'its' instead makes density a property of malice.

rows.jp: 「それでも、あなたは変わらないんですね」
rows.en: “And yet you haven’t changed at all.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "And yet there you are, unchanged."
Taichi: "......"

rows.jp: あっけに取られてしまった。
rows.en: I was taken aback.

ghs.en: I was completely taken aback.

rows.jp: 口ぶりが、まるで好戦的だったのだ。
rows.en: Her tone was downright belligerent.

ghs.en: The way she spoke seemed belligerent.

rows.jp: 「……前から言おうと思っていました」
rows.en: “...I’ve been meaning to tell you this for a long time.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "...I have meant to ask this for some time."

rows.jp: 「先輩はどうして、生きてるんですか？」
rows.en: “Why are you alive?”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Senpai, how come you are alive?"
ghs.assessment: The status-based Japanese address is left unexplained instead of represented in English.

rows.jp: 心臓に楔(くさび)が打ち込まれた。
rows.en: A wedge slammed into my heart.

ghs.en: It was a wedge being driven through my physical heart.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese presents the impact as a wedge driven into his heart. The English's 'was ... being driven' has no clear temporal anchor and 'through' changes penetration into traversal.

highlights.text: It was a wedge being driven through my physical heart.

rows.jp: 『なあ、ひとつ質問なんだけど……どうして今すぐにでも死なないんだ？』
rows.en: *Hey, one question... Why don’t you just die right now?*

ghs.en: 『Say, I got one question though... why don't you just die right this very instant?』

rows.jp: 重なる。
rows.en: The two questions overlapped.

ghs.en: Overlap.

rows.jp: 過去と現在。
rows.en: Past and present.

ghs.en: Past and present,

rows.jp: 交差して。
rows.en: Crossing.

ghs.en: crossing.

rows.jp: まるで、昔投げつけた刃を、今になって不意に投げ返されたような。
rows.en: As though a blade I had hurled long ago had suddenly come flying back at me.

ghs.en: Exactly as if the blade cast off long ago had now suddenly been thrown back at me.

rows.jp: アイロニカルな構図。
rows.en: An ironic symmetry.

ghs.en: What an ironical composition.
ghs.assessment: アイロニカルな構図 means an ironic setup or situation. 'Ironical composition' is not idiomatic for the described reversal.

rows.jp: 「自分に生きる資格があると思っているんですか？」
rows.en: “Do you believe you deserve to live?”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Do you think you have the qualifications to live inside of yourself?"
ghs.assessment: Kiri asks whether he believes he has the right or qualification to live. The English invents the idea of living inside oneself.

highlights.text: the qualifications to live inside of yourself

ghs.en: Taichi: "......"

rows.jp: 「あなたは、黒い」
rows.en: “You’re black inside.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You are... wicked."

rows.jp: 的確な比喩だと思った。
rows.en: I thought it was an apt metaphor.

ghs.en: How the word uses that kanji from my last name. I found that to be an accurate metaphor.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese only says the narrator considers 'black' an apt metaphor. The English inserts an explicit explanation about the kanji in his surname.

highlights.text: How the word uses that kanji from my last name.

rows.jp: 「ヒトじゃない。ヒトに似たものでしかない。ヒトに擬態してる。虫みたいに」
rows.en: “Not human. Just something that looks human. You mimic humans, like an insect.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You're no person. You have nothing more than the semblance of a person. You camouflage yourself as a person. As insects do."

rows.jp: 「擬態して、ヒトに化けて、ヒトを襲う」
rows.en: “You mimic them. Disguise yourself as one. Then prey on them.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Camouflaged, you take the shape of a person, and attack people."

rows.jp: 「あなたは人を傷つけるものです。決して相容れない」
rows.en: “You are something that hurts people. You can never coexist with them.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You are something that hurts people. Completely incompatible."
ghs.assessment: 決して相容れない says he and people can never coexist or be compatible. The English omits both sides of the relation and leaves an adjective as a sentence fragment without a subject or verb.

rows.jp: 「どうしてあなたの適応係数が８０を越えているのか、昔は不思議でした。けどそれはまったくおかしなことじゃない。あなたの中のヒトの部分は、文字通り二割ほどしかない」
rows.en: “I used to wonder why your maladaptation coefficient exceeded eighty. But there is nothing strange about it. The human part of you is, quite literally, only around twenty percent.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "The reason why your Conformity Coefficient crosses over 80 has been inexplicable to me for a long time. But that is absolutely nothing strange. Because the part inside you that is human is literally less than twenty percent and no more."
ghs.assessment: 二割ほど means roughly twenty percent. 'Less than ... and no more' is redundant and incorrectly replaces approximation with an upper bound.

highlights.text: literally less than twenty percent and no more

rows.jp: 饒舌に語る。
rows.en: The words poured from her.

ghs.en: Talking with garrulity,

rows.jp: 今までたくわえられ佐倉霧という様式を覆す、鮮烈なイメージを構築していく。
rows.en: With every word, she demolished the Kiri Sakura I thought I knew and built a vivid new image in her place.

ghs.en: she goes to construct vivid images, overturning the pattern thus far preserved within the name Sakura Kiri.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says her torrent of words constructs a vivid image that overturns the accumulated model of the person called Sakura Kiri. The English instead says a pattern is preserved inside her name and fails to express the reversal coherently.

highlights.text: she goes to construct vivid images, overturning the pattern thus far preserved within the name Sakura Kiri.

rows.jp: 言葉のナイフが、俺の精神を刺そうとしていた。
rows.en: Her words were knives, stabbing at my mind.

ghs.en: The knife that were those words were trying to stab at my very essence.
ghs.assessment: The English uses two incompatible finite verbs and fails subject-verb agreement.

highlights.text: The knife that were those words were trying

rows.jp: 今までは鈍い刃物しか持ち得なかった―――
rows.en: Until now, she had never held anything sharper than a blunt blade—

ghs.en: The dull knife that was all she possessed so far---

rows.jp: 佐倉霧の切り札となって！
rows.en: Now they were Kiri Sakura’s trump card.

ghs.en:
>                                              trump card
Became Sakura Kiri's kiri-fuda!
ghs.assessment: The Japanese exclamation says the once-dull weapon becomes Sakura Kiri's trump card, with the ordinary word 切り札 carrying the prose. The English exposes raw layout markup, reverses the clause order, and inserts unexplained romanized 'kiri-fuda.'

highlights.text:
>                                              trump card
Became Sakura Kiri's kiri-fuda!

rows.jp: 「怪物です」
rows.en: “A monster.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You are a monster."

rows.jp: 「あなたの欺瞞は、怪物の分際で怪物に徹さないところです」
rows.en: “Your hypocrisy is that, for all your monstrosity, you refuse to live as a monster.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Your deceit is that you do not pour your heart and soul into the monster you are, despite your place in society being that of a monster."
ghs.assessment: Kiri says his fraud is that, despite being a monster, he refuses to commit fully to being one. The English invents a monster's 'place in society' and substitutes pouring heart and soul into an identity.

highlights.text: Kiri: "Your deceit is that you do not pour your heart and soul into the monster you are, despite your place in society being that of a monster."

rows.jp: 「人と怪物との間に共感が芽生えて、仲良く幸せに暮らせると思っているんですか？　あなたが人並みの幸せを手に出来ると？」
rows.en: “Do you imagine empathy can grow between human and monster, and that the two can live happily ever after? That you can claim the happiness meant for ordinary people?”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Did you think that empathy could sprout between person and monster, and that you could have a happy life in harmony with others? That you would be able to lay hands on the happiness of the ordinary person?"
ghs.assessment: 幸せを手に出来る means attain or obtain happiness. 'Lay hands on happiness' carries an unintended sense of seizing a physical target.

rows.jp: 「ありえない」
rows.en: “Impossible.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "It will not be."
ghs.assessment: Kiri states that the imagined outcome is impossible. The English turns impossibility into a prediction that it will not occur.

rows.jp: 「世界にわずかしかない優しさは、決してあなたのために取り分けられない。いえ、取り分けられてはならないんです」
rows.en: “The little kindness that exists in this world will never be set aside for you. No—it must never be.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "In this world there is just a little kindness and no more, but there is absolutely no part set aside for you. No, it is simply out of the question that any ever would be set aside."

rows.jp: 「体を食い破って出てくる寄生虫に、愛を抱く人がいないのと一緒です。もしいたとしてもそれは狂人でしょう」
rows.en: “It would be like loving a parasite that bursts out through your flesh. Anyone who did would be insane.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "It is the same as no one would hug with love the parasite that comes out of their body, having devoured its way through it. Should one like that ever even exist, they would be madmen."
ghs.assessment: Kiri says no one would feel love for such a parasite. The English changes the feeling into a physical embrace.

rows.jp: 「あなたはいつも自分のために犠牲になってくれる獲物を捜してる。わたしにはわかります」
rows.en: “You are always hunting for prey that will sacrifice itself for you. I can see that.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You are always searching for game to become a sacrifice for your own benefit. This is clear to me. Up until now, that was something you could suppress. But then the world became like this, the number of persons became insufficient, so your suppression is ineffective."

rows.jp: 「今まではそれは抑えられていた。けど世界がこんなことになって、ヒトの数が少なくなって、あなたの抑えはきかなくなってきてる」
rows.en: “Until now, you kept that urge under control. But with the world reduced to this—with so few humans left—your restraint is beginning to fail.”

rows.jp: 「擬態をする必要がなくなったからです」
rows.en: “Because you no longer need to disguise yourself.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Because the need for camouflage has vanished."

rows.jp: 「傷つけて楽しむため、あなたの目はいつも私たちに注がれている。それもひと思いにではなく、ゆっくりと時間をかけて嬲り尽くそうとしている」
rows.en: “Your eyes are always on us, looking for the pleasure of hurting us. Not all at once, either. You mean to take your time and torment us to the end.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Your eyes are always focused on us, so that you can enjoy the hurting. And it's not something done instantly, you slowly take the time to perform that bullish sexual 'teasing' of yours all the way to the end."
ghs.assessment: Kiri accuses him of slowly tormenting people to exhaustion. The English invents both a bovine quality and a specifically sexual form of teasing.

rows.jp: 「ヒトでもない、怪物でもない」
rows.en: “Neither human nor monster.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Not a person, nor a monster."

rows.jp: 「では何者なんですか？　何者でもないあなたこそ、世界から消えるべきだった。わたしはそう思います」
rows.en: “Then what are you? You, who are nothing at all, are the one who should have disappeared from this world. That is what I believe.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Then who or what are you? You are neither who nor what, that is what you are, just something that ought to have disappeared from the world. That is what I think."
ghs.assessment: 何者でもない means he is nobody or nothing. The paired interrogative pronouns do not form an idiomatic English predicate.

highlights.text: You are neither who nor what

rows.jp: 「大半が悪意に満ちた人類だって、あなた一人の命よりはずっと価値があった。わたしにとってさえ、そうです」
rows.en: “Even humanity, most of it filled with malice, was worth far more than your one life. Even to me.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "The majority of mankind was so full of malice, but even that had a value far greater than your one life. To me, that is the truth."

rows.jp: 「ふたつ、忠告します」
rows.en: “I have two warnings for you.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "I will give two pieces of advice."

rows.jp: 「まずあなたが他者との触れあいの中で本当の人間になれるのだと思っているとしたら、それは間違いです。あり得ません。人間を冒涜する考えです」
rows.en: “First: if you believe that contact with others can make you truly human, you are mistaken. It is impossible. The very idea is an insult to humanity.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "The first, if you believe that within the exchange of touches with other people you will become a real human, you are mistaken. That will not be. Thinking that is to blaspheme humanity. Because I have never seen a more perfect monster than you, Senpai."

rows.jp: 「先輩ほど完璧なバケモノは見たことないですから」
rows.en: “I have never seen a more perfect monster than you.”

rows.jp: 「あなたは掛け値なしの精神異常者。狂人の中の狂人」
rows.en: “You are deranged through and through. A madman among madmen.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "You are, without exaggeration, a psychotic, a deviant of the soul. A madman among madmen."
ghs.assessment: 掛け値なしの精神異常者 supplies one characterization, an unqualified mentally abnormal or deranged person. The English expands it into two diagnoses and adds the metaphysical phrase 'deviant of the soul.'

highlights.text: a psychotic, a deviant of the soul

rows.jp: 「……狂える者たちの頂点です」
rows.en: “...The apex of madness.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "...the crowning jewel of all that go mad."
ghs.assessment: 頂点 is the apex or pinnacle. 'Crowning jewel' is laudatory and ornamental, changing the force of the condemnation.

rows.jp: 「そしてもう一つ。わたしたちに手を出そうとは思わないことです」
rows.en: “And second: do not even think of laying a hand on us.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "And then one more. Do not even think of wanting to lay your hands on us in any sense."
ghs.assessment: The source warns him not to think of making a move on them. The nested 'think of wanting to' is not natural English.

highlights.text: think of wanting to lay your hands

rows.jp: 「もし先輩が生贄を求めてわたしたちに近づくことがあれば……」
rows.en: “If you ever come near us in search of another sacrifice...”

ghs.en: Kiri: "Should you approach us in search for a sacrificial lamb, Senpai..."
ghs.assessment: The fixed phrase is 'in search of,' not 'in search for.'

rows.jp: 最後のひとつきを、霧は繰り出す。
rows.en: Kiri delivered the final thrust.

ghs.en: Kiri unleashes the very final thrust.

rows.jp: 「射殺します」
rows.en: “I will shoot you dead.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "I will shoot to kill."

rows.jp: 「……美希は絶対に、あなたには渡さない」
rows.en: “...You will never have Miki.”

ghs.en: Kiri: "...I will never, ever hand Miki over to you."

rows.jp: 「壊させない！」
rows.en: “I won't let you break her!”

ghs.en: Kiri: "I won't let you break her!"

rows.jp: つかつかと靴音を立てて、脇を通り過ぎる。
rows.en: She strode past me, her shoes clicking sharply.

ghs.en: With the sound of determined footstep, she passes right underarm.
ghs.assessment: Kiri strides past the narrator's side. The English calques the body-part expression and says she passes beneath an armpit.

rows.jp: 軋む扉。締まる扉。
rows.en: The door creaked. The door shut.

ghs.en:
The door creaks.
The door shuts.
ghs.assessment: The source presents two successive beats: the door creaks and then closes. The English omits the closing beat.

rows.jp: 俺は一人になった。
rows.en: I was alone.

ghs.en: I became alone.
ghs.assessment: The Japanese says he was left alone or found himself alone. 'Became alone' is not idiomatic for that change of situation.

ghs.en: Taichi: "......monster..."

rows.jp: 怪物。
rows.en: Monster.

ghs.en: Monster.

rows.jp: 怪物。
rows.en: Monster.

ghs.en: Monster.

rows.jp: 怪物。
rows.en: Monster.

ghs.en: Monster.

rows.jp: 言葉を反芻して、噛みしめる。
rows.en: I ruminated on the word—chewed it over.

ghs.en: I ruminate over the word, and try biting into it.
ghs.assessment: The narrator turns the word over and absorbs its meaning. The English renders the idiom as a literal attempt to bite a word.

rows.jp: 苦み。
rows.en: Bitterness.

ghs.en: Bitter.
ghs.assessment: 苦み is the noun 'bitterness' or 'a bitter taste.' The English supplies an adjective without anything for it to modify.

rows.jp: これは脳の味だ。
rows.en: That was the taste of my brain.

ghs.en: That is the taste of the brain.

rows.jp: 脳がある種の神経伝達物質を分泌し、その味が味覚を司る神経に直接乗って錯覚を起こす。
rows.en: My brain secreted some kind of neurotransmitter, and its taste traveled directly along my gustatory nerves, creating the illusion.

ghs.en:
The brain secretes a certain type of
neurotransmitter, and its flavor rides directly
to the nerves that govern the taste, creating
the illusion.
ghs.assessment: The English preserves intrusive engine line breaks and uses the awkward phrase 'the nerves that govern the taste' where English requires the nerves governing taste or the gustatory nerves.

highlights.text:
The brain secretes a certain type of
neurotransmitter, and its flavor rides directly
to the nerves that govern the taste, creating
the illusion.

rows.jp: 怪物。
rows.en: Monster.

ghs.en: Monster.

rows.jp: いみじくも、自分を表するときの言葉と同じ。
rows.en: Aptly enough, it was the very word I used for myself.

ghs.en:
So exquisite that it's the exact same word
I use to represent myself.
ghs.assessment: いみじくも means aptly or quite appropriately here, not exquisitely. The English also preserves intrusive engine line breaks.

rows.jp: 「いてて」
rows.en: “Ow.”

ghs.en: Taichi: "OwChCh."

rows.jp: ほら、傷む。
rows.en: See? It hurt.

ghs.en: Well look here, it hurts.

rows.jp: 乾いた心がひりつく。
rows.en: My parched heart smarted.

ghs.en: My dried up heart stings.

rows.jp: ささった無数の切片が、苦痛を生み続ける。
rows.en: The countless shards lodged in it went on producing pain.

ghs.en: The countless slices that had been cut into it continue to produce agony.
ghs.assessment: 切片 here are fragments or slivers lodged in the heart. The English turns them into slices that themselves had been cut into the heart, changing both object and action.

highlights.text: slices that had been cut into it

rows.jp: 「まったく……ズケズケと……」
rows.en: “Man... she really came right out with it...”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Dammit... all blunt like that..."

rows.jp: 膝立ちになる。
rows.en: I pushed myself up onto my knees.

ghs.en: I fall to my knees.
ghs.assessment: 膝立ちになる means he rises or moves into an upright kneeling posture. 'Fall to my knees' describes a collapse in the opposite direction.

rows.jp: 立ちくらみがした。
rows.en: I got a head rush.

ghs.en: I became dizzy from vertigo.
ghs.assessment: 立ちくらみ is a head rush or momentary dizziness on changing posture. The English adds a diagnosis of vertigo and redundantly says dizziness came from dizziness.

rows.jp: 「あーいて……いてて。いたいけど」
rows.en: “Agh, ow... ow. It hurts, but—”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Awww ouch... ouch ouch. But it hurts..."

rows.jp: どれも、致命傷ではない。
rows.en: None of the wounds was mortal.

ghs.en: But none of them are fatal wounds.

rows.jp: 霧のナイフは、俺の心を効果的に貫いてはいない。
rows.en: Kiri’s knives hadn’t cut deep enough.

ghs.en: Kiri's knife did not successfully penetrate into my heart.

rows.jp: 表面に細かな傷をつけただけだ。
rows.en: They had only nicked the surface.

ghs.en: It just left thin gashes on the surface.
ghs.assessment: 細かな傷 are small, superficial scratches or wounds. 'Gashes' denotes deep cuts and contradicts the point that the damage is only on the surface.

rows.jp: 痛みはあるが。
rows.en: It hurt.

ghs.en: There's pain but,

rows.jp: 児戯に属した。
rows.en: But it was child's play.

ghs.en: it is of the genus of mere child's play.

rows.jp: かつて俺が受けてきた『攻撃』は、こんなものではない。
rows.en: The ‘attacks’ I had endured before were nothing like this.

ghs.en: The... Attack that I took in my beginnings was nothing like this.
ghs.assessment: かつて means in the past or once. It does not specifically locate the attacks in his beginnings or childhood.

rows.jp: だが久々に攻撃を受けた気がする。
rows.en: Still, it felt like ages since anyone had attacked me.

ghs.en: But there's this feeling that I haven't taken an attack in a long time.

rows.jp: 適度な攻撃は、適度な緊張感を呼ぶ。
rows.en: A measured attack produces a measured tension.

ghs.en: A moderate attack that invokes a moderate strain.
ghs.assessment: The English turns the main predicate into a relative clause and leaves the sentence without a finite verb governing its subject.

highlights.text: A moderate attack that invokes a moderate strain.

rows.jp: 酩酊に近い状態か。
rows.en: Perhaps it was something like intoxication.

ghs.en: Is that sort of like drunkenness?

rows.jp: その場に横になる。
rows.en: I lay down where I was.

ghs.en: I end up laying down on that spot.
ghs.assessment: The intransitive present participle is 'lying down'; 'laying' requires an object.

rows.jp: 「……射殺せるなら……そうしてくれ……」
rows.en: “...If you can shoot me dead... then do it...”

ghs.en: Taichi: "...if you can shoot me to death... then please do so..."

rows.jp: 「いっそ楽にしてくれよ～っと♪」
rows.en: “Might as well put me out of my misery♪”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Please release me from my pleee～asure!♪"
ghs.assessment: 楽にしてくれ asks to be put out of his misery or relieved of suffering. The English chooses 'pleasure,' reversing pain relief into release from enjoyment.

rows.jp: 悪くない、気分だった。
rows.en: It felt pretty good.

ghs.en: This mood wasn't bad at all.
